newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish bourse seen falling slightly next week.
newsitem.headline: Polish bourse seen falling slightly next week.

text.p: Polish shares are seen falling slightly next week as investors have apparently decided to pause after recent buying at a discount.
The main market has seen two one-day jumps of over three percent this week and last week after a 14.6-percent fall.
"Nobody wants to buy now, thinking the market is a little too expensive," said Pawel Tarnowski, an analyst at Raiffeisen Capital & Investment. @

But analysts did not expect a repeat of the drop during the final two thirds of October, saying the main market, currently at 13,874.8 points, would likely not fall below 13,000 points, or at worst, below October 29's low at above 12,800 points.
The main market's WIG index rose 2.8 percent this week, buoyed in part by Russian President Boris Yeltsin's successful heart operation on Tuesday.
Analysts said recent buying was likely done by large institutional investors, signalled by the recent low number of orders and gains by large-cap, fundamentally sound stocks. @
Three such stocks -- Zywiec, BRE and Polifarb Wroclaw -- led the main market this week, up 20.8 percent, 13.8 percent and 11.2 percent respectively.

Analysts said that at the middle of next week investors would be watching the Senate's vote on 1997's tax rates after parliament's lower house recent vote to cut taxes for low earners, seen as inflationary and helping cause market falls.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski is expected to overturn the measure if the Senate does not do so first.
Analysts said a healthy supply of primary market offers could also help dampen demand next week. @
"They're all small offers but most of them are pretty attractive," said Krzysztof Rogalski, an analyst at Bank Staropolski brokerage.

Analysts said next week's inflation number for October, due on Friday, would likely not have a significant effect on the market as the central bank had already said no interest rate cut was forthcoming.

But some said this week's news that food prices had risen only 0.3 percent from September's final 10 days to October's final 10 was a good sign, perhaps helping to keep 1996 inflation as low as 18 percent. @
"At least it (the low food-price rise) suggests that maybe some time in the future there might be room for a rate cut," said Wojciech Bialek, an analyst at Magnus brokerage.
Markets are closed on Monday for the Independence Day holiday. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
